title: Grade 4 SOCIAL STUDIES — 5.1 Good Citizenship in School

pages.lesson:
PAGE 1: Overview

OVERVIEW
========

A citizen is a person who belongs to a country. In school, good citizenship is shown in daily behaviour. In this sub-strand you will name the qualities of a good citizen, practise them, and explain why they make school peaceful and successful.

## Strand 5.0: Citizenship and Governance in Kenya
Sub-strand 5.1: Good Citizenship in School
Suggested lessons: 4

## Learning outcomes
By the end of the sub-strand, the learner should be able to:
a) identify qualities of a good citizen in school
b) develop qualities of good citizenship in school
c) appreciate qualities of good citizenship in school

## Key inquiry questions
1. How can we demonstrate good citizenship in school?

## Core competencies
• Citizenship: Learners role-play qualities of a good citizen in school

## Values
• Unity: Learners design a poster with qualities of a good citizen in school

## Pertinent and contemporary issues
• Social cohesion: Learners develop harmonious coexistence as they discuss how to become a good citizen in school

## Links to other learning areas
• English: Learners apply writing skills as they write an essay on a good digital citizen (using technology in a positive way) and share the essays in class.

## Source
• KICD Grade 4 Social Studies Curriculum Design (Revised 2024) — Strand 5.0 Citizenship and Governance in Kenya, Sub-strand 5.1 Good Citizenship in School
• KICD Grade 4 Social Studies radio lesson: Qualities of Good Citizenship in School

PAGE 2: Lesson 1: Qualities of a good citizen in school

LESSON 1: QUALITIES OF A GOOD CITIZEN IN SCHOOL
===============================================

## What you will learn
• Explain the meaning of citizen and citizenship.
• Identify qualities of a good citizen in school.

Curriculum outcomes: a) identify qualities of a good citizen in school

## Introduction
Two learners find a lost jumper. One hides it in a bag. The other takes it to the teacher. Both are learners in the same school, but only one is acting as a good citizen.

## Notes
A citizen is a person who belongs to a particular place or country. Citizenship is belonging to that country and taking part in its life, including the rights and the duties that belong with it. School is one of the first places where you practise citizenship.

A good citizen in school can be recognised by qualities. A quality is a feature of a person's behaviour that shows again and again.

### Qualities to look for
- Kindness: helping a learner who has fallen or who is new
- Honesty: telling the truth and returning what is not yours
- Care: looking after books, desks, younger learners and the compound
- Obedience: following lawful school rules and teachers' instructions
- Responsibility: doing your duty without being hunted for
- Hard work: finishing classwork and duties carefully
- Humility: not boasting or looking down on others
- Tolerance: accepting learners who speak another language, who learn differently, or who come from another community
- Generosity: sharing what can rightly be shared, such as a rubber or a place on the bench
- Peacefulness: solving disagreements with words, not fists

You can find these qualities in storybooks, in the school rules, and by watching learners whom the class trusts. Digital or print resources, such as a textbook page or a short article the teacher shows, can add examples. Write the quality and a school example beside it, so that the word does not stay abstract.

Qualities are choices. A learner is not born kind or born selfish. Each day gives a fresh chance to practise.

## Key words
• citizen — a person who belongs to a country or a community
• citizenship — belonging to a country and taking part in its rights and duties
• quality — a feature of behaviour that a person shows again and again

## Worked examples

### Example 1
A learner returns a found pen to the owner. Which quality is this?

Working:
1. The pen was not theirs.
2. They gave it back instead of keeping it.

Answer: Honesty.

### Example 2
A learner refuses to sit with a classmate because of the classmate's home language. Which quality is missing?

Working:
1. The classmate is being excluded for a difference.
2. Accepting differences is tolerance.

Answer: Tolerance.

## Activity: Brainstorm good citizenship
You will need: Exercise book, Textbook or other print material, Manila paper
1. Brainstorm qualities of a good citizen in school.
2. Use a textbook or another print or digital resource the teacher provides to add any quality the group missed.
3. Beside each quality, write one action a learner can do this week.
4. Share the chart with the class and agree a class list.

## Practice
1. What is a citizen?
2. Name five qualities of a good citizen in school.
3. Give one school example of responsibility.

## Summary
• A citizen belongs to a country. School is a place to practise citizenship.
• Good qualities include honesty, kindness, responsibility, hard work and tolerance.
• Each quality should be matched with a real action.

### Answers to practice
1. A person who belongs to a particular country or place.
2. Any five: kindness, honesty, care, obedience, responsibility, hard work, humility, tolerance, generosity and peacefulness.
3. Doing a class duty, such as sweeping or handing in work, without being reminded.

PAGE 3: Lesson 2: Choosing good actions

LESSON 2: CHOOSING GOOD ACTIONS
===============================

## What you will learn
• Distinguish good qualities from poor ones.
• Use simple questions to choose a good action.

Curriculum outcomes: a) identify qualities of a good citizen in school; b) develop qualities of good citizenship in school

## Introduction
Before you hide a classmate's book as a joke, you can pause. A short question can stop a small meanness from becoming a habit.

## Notes
Knowing the words is not the same as living them. Good citizenship grows when you notice a choice and pick the better action.

### Poor qualities to refuse
These behaviours damage school life:

- Disobedience to lawful rules
- Laziness that leaves duties to others
- Rudeness to learners, teachers and workers
- Irresponsibility, such as losing school books and shrugging
- Bullying: hurting, threatening or leaving someone out on purpose
- Greed: taking more than your share
- Selfishness: refusing to help when you safely can

A bully is not showing strength. Bullying is a failure of kindness and peacefulness. The learner who is targeted should tell a trusted teacher. The learners who watch should not laugh. Laughing grows the harm.

### Four questions before you act
1. Will my teacher be happy with what I am about to do?
2. Will my parents or guardians be happy with it?
3. Will it help other learners?
4. Will it help me learn?

If the answer to these questions is no, choose another action. The questions also work online. A good digital citizen uses a phone or computer in a positive way: no insults, no sharing of another person's photo without permission, no passing on rumours, and asking an adult when a message feels wrong. Technology does not cancel kindness.

Developing a quality means repeating the good action until it becomes normal. One honest act is a start. Honest acts every week build a reputation.

## Key words
• bullying — hurting, threatening or deliberately leaving someone out
• digital citizen — a person who uses phones and computers in a way that helps, and does not harm, other people
• reputation — what people have learned to expect from your behaviour

## Worked examples

### Example 1
A learner wants to forward a classmate's photo to a group chat to mock them. Which questions should stop this?

Working:
1. Ask whether teachers and parents would approve.
2. Ask whether it helps the classmate.

Answer: No. It is unkind, and a good digital citizen does not share someone's photo to mock them.

### Example 2
Sort these words into good and poor qualities: rude, hardworking, greedy, humble.

Working:
1. Hardworking and humble help the school.
2. Rude and greedy harm it.

Answer: Good: hardworking, humble. Poor: rude, greedy.

## Activity: Sort the qualities
You will need: Word cards, Exercise book
1. The teacher reads a mixed list, such as kind, disobedient, honest, lazy, caring, rude, peaceful, bully, hardworking and selfish.
2. Each group sorts the words into good qualities and poor qualities.
3. Choose one poor quality and role-play a better action in its place.
4. Write the four questions you will ask yourself before a difficult choice, including a choice made on a phone.

## Practice
1. Name three poor qualities a learner should refuse.
2. What is a good digital citizen?
3. State two questions to ask yourself before you act.

## Summary
• Poor qualities such as bullying and greed harm the school.
• Four questions can guide a choice, including online.
• A quality grows when the good action is repeated.

### Answers to practice
1. Any three: disobedience, laziness, rudeness, irresponsibility, bullying, greed and selfishness.
2. A person who uses technology kindly: no insults, no mocking photos, and asking an adult when something feels wrong.
3. Any two: Will my teacher be happy? Will my parents be happy? Will it help other learners? Will it help me learn?

PAGE 4: Lesson 3: Showing good citizenship

LESSON 3: SHOWING GOOD CITIZENSHIP
==================================

## What you will learn
• Role-play qualities of a good citizen.
• Explain how good citizenship helps the whole school.

Curriculum outcomes: b) develop qualities of good citizenship in school; c) appreciate qualities of good citizenship in school

## Introduction
A quality that stays on a poster does not sweep the classroom. Citizenship becomes real when learners act it out in ordinary moments, then keep acting that way when the play is over.

## Notes
Developing a quality means practising it on purpose. Role-play is a safe way to rehearse. One learner plays a new pupil who cannot find the toilet. Another plays a guide. The class watches for kindness, clear speech and patience. After the scene, they name the quality and say what they would copy tomorrow.

### What changes when many learners practise
- Learning improves, because time is not lost to fights and noise.
- Property lasts, because people care for books, taps and desks.
- There is peace. New learners settle faster.
- Duties such as cleaning are finished, so the compound stays healthy.
- Learners trust one another enough to share ideas in class.

Appreciating good citizenship means noticing it and thanking it. If a classmate picks up litter that is not theirs, say so. Praise teaches the school what to copy. Appreciating also means refusing to mock a learner who is trying to be honest or kind.

A role model is a person whose behaviour is worth copying. In the community this may be a teacher, a faith leader, a nurse, a farmer who deals honestly, or an older learner. When you talk with a role model, ask what they do when telling the truth is difficult. Their answer is more useful than a slogan.

Good citizenship at school and at home match. A learner who is gentle at school and cruel to a younger sibling has not yet made the quality their own. Practise in both places.

## Key words
• role-play — acting out a situation in order to practise how to behave
• role model — a person whose good behaviour is worth copying
• appreciate — to notice the value of something and show respect for it

## Worked examples

### Example 1
During role-play, a learner laughs at a classmate who is pretending to be lost. What should the group do?

Working:
1. The laugh is unkind.
2. The scene was meant to practise care.

Answer: Stop the mockery, apologise, and replay the scene with kindness.

### Example 2
Give two results of good citizenship for a school.

Working:
1. Think about learning and about safety.

Answer: Learners learn better because there is order, and people and property are safer.

## Activity: Role-play a good citizen
You will need: Space to act, Word cards of qualities
1. Each group picks one quality: honesty, kindness, tolerance or responsibility.
2. Role-play a short school scene that shows the quality.
3. The watching group names the quality and one action they will copy.
4. If a community role model visits, ask them how they practise good citizenship and write two points from their answer.
5. Thank learners who showed the quality during the lesson itself.

## Practice
1. What is a role model?
2. Give two ways good citizenship helps a school.
3. How can you appreciate a classmate who tells the truth?

## Summary
• Role-play is a way to practise qualities before you need them.
• Good citizenship improves learning, safety and peace.
• Appreciate the learners and adults who already show the qualities.

### Answers to practice
1. A person whose good behaviour is worth copying.
2. Any two: better learning, safer people, property that lasts, peace, and finished duties.
3. Notice what they did and thank them, instead of mocking them.

PAGE 5: Lesson 4: A poster and an essay on citizenship

LESSON 4: A POSTER AND AN ESSAY ON CITIZENSHIP
==============================================

## What you will learn
• Design a poster of good citizenship qualities.
• Write a short essay on being a good citizen, including online.

Curriculum outcomes: b) develop qualities of good citizenship in school; c) appreciate qualities of good citizenship in school

## Introduction
A poster on the classroom wall can remind a tired class what they agreed to be. An essay makes you explain the same ideas in your own sentences.

## Notes
Designing a poster brings the qualities together. A clear poster has a title, such as 'A good citizen in our school', four or five qualities, and a small drawing for each one. Too many words make it hard to read from the back of the room. One short line under each picture is enough: 'I return what I find.' 'I share the bench.' 'I refuse to bully.'

Work on the poster as a group. Unity here means listening to one another's ideas and combining them, not letting one learner draw everything while others watch. Hang the poster where the class will see it during disputes as well as during lessons.

### The essay
An essay is a short piece of writing with a beginning, a middle and an ending.

- Beginning: say what a good citizen is.
- Middle: describe three qualities and one example each. Include one paragraph on a good digital citizen, because phones and computers are part of school life. Say that you will not insult people online, will not share private photos, and will tell an adult about harmful messages.
- Ending: say why you want to be that kind of citizen, at school and at home.

Read the essay aloud to a partner. The partner listens for one quality you explained well and one sentence that is unclear. Improve the unclear sentence. Sharing the writing is part of learning, not a competition to embarrass anyone.

Appreciating the qualities means you are willing to be corrected by your own poster. If the poster says 'I do not bully' and you exclude someone at break, the poster has caught you. Go back and repair the action.

## Key words
• poster — a large notice with a short message and pictures
• essay — a short piece of writing with a beginning, a middle and an ending
• unity — working together as one group

## Worked examples

### Example 1
A poster lists twelve long paragraphs. Why will it fail as a poster?

Working:
1. People read a poster quickly, often from a distance.

Answer: It has too many words. A poster needs a title, a few qualities and short lines.

### Example 2
Where in an essay should a learner explain online kindness?

Working:
1. The beginning defines a good citizen.
2. Examples belong in the middle.

Answer: In the middle, as one of the examples of good citizenship.

## Activity: Poster and essay
You will need: Manila paper, Crayons, Exercise book
1. In groups, design a poster with qualities of a good citizen in school.
2. Give each quality a short line and a picture. Display the poster.
3. Write an essay on qualities of a good citizen, including a good digital citizen, and share it with a partner.
4. Improve one sentence after your partner's comment.
5. Choose one quality from your poster to practise for the rest of the week.

## Practice
1. What should a citizenship poster contain?
2. Name the three parts of a short essay.
3. Write one sentence a good digital citizen would agree with.

## Summary
• A poster reminds the class of a few clear qualities.
• An essay explains the qualities, including kind use of technology.
• The poster should match how you actually behave.

### Answers to practice
1. A title, a few qualities, a short line for each, and simple pictures.
2. A beginning, a middle and an ending.
3. I will not insult people online or share their photos without permission.
pages.quiz:
REVISION QUIZ — 5.1 GOOD CITIZENSHIP IN SCHOOL
========================================

Answer all the questions, then mark yourself on the Answers tab.

1. A citizen is:
   A. A person who belongs to a country
   B. Only a school prefect
   C. A type of industry
   D. A raw material

2. Which list shows qualities of a good citizen in school?
   A. Honest, kind, hardworking and tolerant
   B. Rude, greedy, lazy and selfish
   C. Bullying, gossip and noise
   D. Poaching, waste and litter

3. Returning a found rubber to its owner shows:
   A. Greed
   B. Honesty
   C. Laziness
   D. Bullying

4. Bullying is:
   A. A sign of a good leader
   B. Hurting, threatening or leaving someone out on purpose
   C. A school subject
   D. The same as hard work

5. A good digital citizen will:
   A. Share a classmate's photo to mock them
   B. Send insults because they are online
   C. Refuse to insult people and ask an adult about harmful messages
   D. Hide the phone from every teacher forever

6. Which question helps you choose a good action?
   A. Will this help other learners?
   B. Will I get away with it?
   C. Can I blame someone else?
   D. Will it make a classmate afraid?

7. Role-play is useful because:
   A. It lets you practise a quality safely
   B. It replaces all school rules
   C. It is a way to mock classmates
   D. It ends the need to be honest afterwards

8. When many learners practise good citizenship, the school:
   A. Becomes more peaceful and learning improves
   B. Loses all its property
   C. Stops teaching
   D. Has more bullying

9. A role model is:
   A. A person whose good behaviour is worth copying
   B. Anyone who is famous
   C. A learner who bullies and is feared
   D. A broken school rule

10. Why should a citizenship poster use few words?
pages.answers:
ANSWERS — 5.1 GOOD CITIZENSHIP IN SCHOOL
========================================

1. A. A person who belongs to a country
   Citizenship begins with belonging to a country and taking part in its life.

2. A. Honest, kind, hardworking and tolerant
   Honesty, kindness, hard work and tolerance help the school community.

3. B. Honesty
   Giving back what is not yours is honesty.

4. B. Hurting, threatening or leaving someone out on purpose
   Bullying harms another learner and fails the qualities of kindness and peace.

5. C. Refuse to insult people and ask an adult about harmful messages
   Using technology in a positive way is part of good citizenship.

6. A. Will this help other learners?
   Good citizenship asks whether the action helps others and fits what trusted adults expect.

7. A. It lets you practise a quality safely
   Acting a scene is practice for real behaviour.

8. A. Becomes more peaceful and learning improves
   Order, care of property and peace give more time for learning.

9. A. A person whose good behaviour is worth copying
   We copy role models because their behaviour is good, not merely because they are well known.

10. So that people can read the message quickly from a distance.
   A poster is a reminder, not a full essay.

4. If a community role model visits, ask them how they practise good citizenship and write two points from their answer.
5. Thank learners who showed the quality during the lesson itself.

## Practice
1. What is a role model?
2. Give two ways good citizenship helps a school.
3. How can you appreciate a classmate who tells the truth?

## Summary
• Role-play is a way to practise qualities before you need them.
• Good citizenship improves learning, safety and peace.
• Appreciate the learners and adults who already show the qualities.

### Answers to practice
1. A person whose good behaviour is worth copying.
2. Any two: better learning, safer people, property that lasts, peace, and finished duties.
3. Notice what they did and thank them, instead of mocking them.

studyPages.title: Lesson 4: A poster and an essay on citizenship
studyPages.body:
LESSON 4: A POSTER AND AN ESSAY ON CITIZENSHIP
==============================================

## What you will learn
• Design a poster of good citizenship qualities.
• Write a short essay on being a good citizen, including online.

Curriculum outcomes: b) develop qualities of good citizenship in school; c) appreciate qualities of good citizenship in school

## Introduction
A poster on the classroom wall can remind a tired class what they agreed to be. An essay makes you explain the same ideas in your own sentences.

## Notes
Designing a poster brings the qualities together. A clear poster has a title, such as 'A good citizen in our school', four or five qualities, and a small drawing for each one. Too many words make it hard to read from the back of the room. One short line under each picture is enough: 'I return what I find.' 'I share the bench.' 'I refuse to bully.'

Work on the poster as a group. Unity here means listening to one another's ideas and combining them, not letting one learner draw everything while others watch. Hang the poster where the class will see it during disputes as well as during lessons.

### The essay
An essay is a short piece of writing with a beginning, a middle and an ending.

- Beginning: say what a good citizen is.
- Middle: describe three qualities and one example each. Include one paragraph on a good digital citizen, because phones and computers are part of school life. Say that you will not insult people online, will not share private photos, and will tell an adult about harmful messages.
- Ending: say why you want to be that kind of citizen, at school and at home.

Read the essay aloud to a partner. The partner listens for one quality you explained well and one sentence that is unclear. Improve the unclear sentence. Sharing the writing is part of learning, not a competition to embarrass anyone.

Appreciating the qualities means you are willing to be corrected by your own poster. If the poster says 'I do not bully' and you exclude someone at break, the poster has caught you. Go back and repair the action.

## Key words
• poster — a large notice with a short message and pictures
• essay — a short piece of writing with a beginning, a middle and an ending
• unity — working together as one group

## Worked examples

### Example 1
A poster lists twelve long paragraphs. Why will it fail as a poster?

Working:
1. People read a poster quickly, often from a distance.

Answer: It has too many words. A poster needs a title, a few qualities and short lines.

### Example 2
Where in an essay should a learner explain online kindness?

Working:
1. The beginning defines a good citizen.
2. Examples belong in the middle.

Answer: In the middle, as one of the examples of good citizenship.

## Activity: Poster and essay
You will need: Manila paper, Crayons, Exercise book
1. In groups, design a poster with qualities of a good citizen in school.
2. Give each quality a short line and a picture. Display the poster.
3. Write an essay on qualities of a good citizen, including a good digital citizen, and share it with a partner.
4. Improve one sentence after your partner's comment.
5. Choose one quality from your poster to practise for the rest of the week.

## Practice
1. What should a citizenship poster contain?
2. Name the three parts of a short essay.
3. Write one sentence a good digital citizen would agree with.

## Summary
• A poster reminds the class of a few clear qualities.
• An essay explains the qualities, including kind use of technology.
• The poster should match how you actually behave.

### Answers to practice
1. A title, a few qualities, a short line for each, and simple pictures.
2. A beginning, a middle and an ending.
3. I will not insult people online or share their photos without permission.

questions.question: A citizen is:
options: A person who belongs to a country
questions.explanation: Citizenship begins with belonging to a country and taking part in its life.

questions.question: Which list shows qualities of a good citizen in school?
questions.explanation: Honesty, kindness, hard work and tolerance help the school community.

questions.question: Returning a found rubber to its owner shows:
questions.explanation: Giving back what is not yours is honesty.

questions.question: Bullying is:
options: A sign of a good leader
Hurting, threatening or leaving someone out on purpose
questions.explanation: Bullying harms another learner and fails the qualities of kindness and peace.

questions.question: A good digital citizen will:
options: Share a classmate's photo to mock them
Send insults because they are online
Refuse to insult people and ask an adult about harmful messages
Hide the phone from every teacher forever
questions.explanation: Using technology in a positive way is part of good citizenship.

questions.question: Which question helps you choose a good action?
options: Will I get away with it?
Will it make a classmate afraid?
questions.explanation: Good citizenship asks whether the action helps others and fits what trusted adults expect.

questions.question: Role-play is useful because:
options: It lets you practise a quality safely
It is a way to mock classmates
It ends the need to be honest afterwards
questions.explanation: Acting a scene is practice for real behaviour.

questions.question: When many learners practise good citizenship, the school:
options: Becomes more peaceful and learning improves
questions.explanation: Order, care of property and peace give more time for learning.

questions.question: A role model is:
options: A person whose good behaviour is worth copying
A learner who bullies and is feared
questions.explanation: We copy role models because their behaviour is good, not merely because they are well known.

questions.question: Why should a citizenship poster use few words?
questions.answer: So that people can read the message quickly from a distance.
questions.explanation: A poster is a reminder, not a full essay.
